references.text: Shortly before this, the disciples had shown Jesus two swords ([ref:Luk 22:38|Luke 22:38]), which explains why they now ask whether they should use swords to defend him.

In Matthew's parallel account, one of those with Jesus cuts off the ear of the high priest's servant with a sword ([ref:Matt 26:51|Matthew 26:51]), which is the immediate action following the question in Luke.
Mark's parallel account also tells of the one who stood there and drew his sword and struck at the high priest's servant ([ref:Mark 14:47|Mark 14:47]).
John identifies the one who used the sword as Simon Peter, and names the servant as Malchus ([ref:Joh 18:10-11|John 18:10-11]). Jesus commands Peter to put his sword back in its sheath.
The subsequent action in [ref:Luk 22:50-51|Luke 22:50-51] shows that one of the disciples actually struck with a sword, and Jesus healed the ear – an answer to the question they asked in verse 49.

Jesus rebukes the use of swords and says that all who take up the sword will perish by the sword ([ref:Matt 26:52-54|Matthew 26:52-54]). This shows that the answer to the disciples' question in Luke 22:49 is no – God's will must be fulfilled.

The expression "to strike with a sword" has its background in the Old Testament, where God acts against those He intends ([ref:2 Mos 21:13|Exodus 21:13]), and here the disciples use the verb πατάσσω (strike), which is also used in the Septuagint regarding God's intervention.

The prophecy in [ref:Sak 13:7|Zechariah 13:7] about striking the shepherd so that the sheep are scattered forms the background for the arrest scene. The disciples try to prevent what has been prophesied.

Isaiah warns against those who kindle their own fire and surround themselves with burning arrows ([ref:Jes 50:11|Isaiah 50:11]) – an image of human defense instead of trusting in the Lord's salvation, parallel to the disciples' desire to take up swords.
